**Recurrence.** If $a_{n-1} = p(n-1) + q$ with $0 \le q < n-1$, then writing $a_{n-1}$ in base $n-1$ gives digits $p, q$. Reading them in base $n$ gives $pn + q$, so
$$a_n = a_{n-1} + \left\lfloor \frac{a_{n-1}}{n-1} \right\rfloor + 2.$$
This holds whenever $p < n$, which is true here since $a_n$ grows roughly like $n\log n$.

**Linear phases.** Suppose $a_n = sn - C$ for some integer $s$ and constant $C$. Then
$$\left\lfloor \frac{a_{n-1}}{n-1} \right\rfloor = s - \left\lceil \frac{C}{n-1} \right\rceil,$$
so the increment is $d_n = s + 2 - \lceil C/(n-1) \rceil$.

- While $1 < C/(n-1) \le 2$, the increment is $s$, so the line $a_n = sn - C$ continues.
- When $n-1 = C$, the increment becomes $s+1$. The new line is $a_n = (s+1)n - C'$ with $C' = 2C$, since at $n = C+1$ we have $a_n = s(C+1) - C + 1$.

So slope $s$ with constant $C$ holds for $n \in (C/2,\, C]$, and the next phase has slope $s+1$ and constant $2C$.

**Phases.** Checking $a_{13}, \dots, a_{23}$ directly confirms $a_n = 6n - 24$ on the first phase. The phases are then:

| Slope $s$ | $C$ | Range of $n$ |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 24 | $(12, 24]$ |
| 7 | 48 | $(24, 48]$ |
| 8 | 96 | $(48, 96]$ |
| 9 | 192 | $(96, 192]$ |
| 10 | 384 | $(192, 384]$ |
| 11 | 768 | $(384, 768]$ |
| 12 | 1536 | $(768, 1536]$ |
| 13 | 3072 | $(1536, 3072]$ |

Spot checks: $a_{25} = 127 = 7\cdot 25 - 48$, and $a_{49} = 296 = 8\cdot 49 - 96$.

**Evaluation.** Since $1536 < 2013 \le 3072$, the phase is slope 13 with $C = 3072$:
$$a_{2013} = 13 \cdot 2013 - 3072 = 26169 - 3072 = 23097.$$

ANSWER: 23097
